paragraphs.text: Monilethrix is a rare dominant hair disease characterized by beaded or moniliform hair, which results from periodic thinning of the hair shaft and shows a high propensity to excess weathering and fracturing (Winter et al., 1997). Monilethrix-2 is caused by mutation in the type II hair cortex keratin hHb1; the phenotype can be particularly variable within a family, ranging from dystrophic alopecia with follicular keratosis to moniliform hair detectable only by electron microscopy (Winter et al., 1998).

paragraphs.text: Winter et al. (1998) reported a French family with monilethrix in which affected members showed a particularly variable phenotype. The pedigree included 2 infants, one with pronounced dystrophic alopecia, follicular keratosis, and clear-cut moniliform hair, and the other with no hair loss at all and moniliform hair detectable only by electron microscopy. An adult family member had no clinically or electron microscopically detectable symptoms but had clear historical proof of the disease.

paragraphs.text: Winter et al. (1997) studied 2 unrelated monilethrix families and a single patient. Affected members of one family and the single patient carried the prevalent glu410-to-lys (E410K) mutation in the type II hair keratin hHb6 (see MNLIX1). In affected individuals of the second family, they identified a lysine substitution of the corresponding glutamic acid residue, glu403 (E403K), in the type II hair keratin hHb1, suggesting that this site represents a mutational hotspot in these highly related type II hair keratins. Because hHb1 and hHb6 are largely coexpressed in cortical trichocytes of the hair shaft, the authors concluded that monilethrix is a disease of the hair cortex.

paragraphs.text: Winter et al. (1998) noted that pathogenic mutations in hHb6 and hHb1 had until then been restricted to a highly conserved glutamic acid residue, designated by them as glu413 (glu117 of the 2B subdomain), in the EIATYRRLLEGEE helix termination motif, substituted either by lysine or, less frequently, by aspartic acid. In a French family with a variable monilethrix phenotype, they identified a novel glu402-to-lys (E402K) mutation in hHb1, affecting another highly conserved glutamic acid residue (glu106 of the 2B subdomain) in the same motif.

agent.process_note: Both papers are abstracts only, and I read both in full. They name the gene hHb1, a type II hair cortex keratin, and give mutations only at the protein level: Glu403Lys in 1997 and Glu402Lys in 1998. The symbol KRT81 and the absence of a gene MIM number reflect that no HGNC reference data was supplied. Neither abstract gives nucleotide changes, family sizes, or explicit segregation data. Neither states zygosity for the hHb1 mutations directly. The 1997 abstract calls the hHb6 mutations heterozygous, and both papers describe dominant transmission. Residue numbering differs between the two papers (Glu403 in 1997; the same site is called Glu413 in 1998), and I describe this without reconciling it.
